query: Consider a homogenized Al0.7CoCrFeNi eutectic alloy initially possessing a dual-phase lamellar structure (FCC/B2) that is strong yet brittle due to stress concentration at incoherent interfaces. The goal is to overcome the strength-ductility trade-off. A hypothesis is proposed involving a High-Pressure and High-Temperature (HPHT) treatment using a hexahedron-anvil apparatus. Predict that applying approximately 6 GPa at 1473 K for 2 hours will induce a topological transformation of the lamellae into a hierarchically patterned microstructure with coherent interfaces. This structure is hypothesized to facilitate multiple deformation mechanisms (dislocation transfer, stacking faults, twinning) and homogeneous strain distribution, effectively arresting interfacial cracking. The mechanism relies on the coherent interface allowing dislocation transfer to alleviate stress. The boundary condition requires that the pressure and temperature are sufficient to induce this specific topological change but not so high as to cause phase instability. A discriminating measurement should compare the fracture surface morphology (isolated microcracks vs. elongated cracks) and the evolution of geometrically necessary dislocation (GND) densities between the treated sample and the baseline, specifically checking if the GND densities of both phases converge at high strain. Falsification would involve showing that conventional thermal-mechanical treatments fail to produce the same hierarchical coherence or GND homogenization.

generation.hypothesis: Applying 6 GPa at 1473 K for 2 hours to a homogenized Al0.7CoCrFeNi eutectic alloy will induce a topological transformation of the incoherent FCC/B2 lamellar interfaces into a hierarchically patterned microstructure with coherent interfaces, thereby enabling dislocation transfer and homogeneous strain distribution to overcome the strength-ductility trade-off.
generation.material_initial_state: Homogenized Al0.7CoCrFeNi eutectic alloy with a dual-phase lamellar structure (FCC/B2) characterized by incoherent interfaces, resulting in high strength but brittleness due to stress concentration.
generation.intervention: High-Pressure and High-Temperature (HPHT) treatment using a hexahedron-anvil apparatus.
generation.conditions: Pressure: ~6 GPa; Temperature: ~1473 K; Duration: 2 hours.
generation.structural_mediator: Topological transformation of lamellar interfaces from incoherent to coherent, establishing a hierarchically patterned microstructure.
generation.mechanism: Coherent interfaces facilitate dislocation transfer between FCC and B2 phases, promoting multiple deformation mechanisms (dislocation glide, stacking fault formation, twinning) and homogeneous strain distribution, which arrests interfacial cracking by alleviating stress concentrations.
generation.predicted_outcome: Significant increase in ductility without substantial loss of strength, evidenced by elongated crack propagation on fracture surfaces and convergent Geometrically Necessary Dislocation (GND) densities in both phases at high strain.
generation.baseline: The untreated Al0.7CoCrFeNi alloy exhibiting isolated microcracks at incoherent interfaces and divergent GND densities between phases under strain.
generation.boundary: The pressure and temperature must be sufficient to drive the topological interface transformation but remain below the threshold for phase instability or decomposition of the eutectic structure.
generation.uncertainty: While HPHT is known to enhance diffusion and interface coherence in other systems, the specific topological transformation of FCC/B2 lamellae in this specific high-entropy alloy composition at exactly 6 GPa/1473 K has not been definitively established; there is a risk that the pressure may induce a different phase transformation (e.g., to BCC or amorphous) rather than the desired coherent lamellar restructuring.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Al0.7CoCrFeNi samples: Set A undergoes the proposed HPHT treatment (6 GPa, 1473 K, 2h), and Set B undergoes a conventional thermal-mechanical treatment (e.g., annealing at 1473 K at 0.1 MPa) for the same duration. Both sets are subjected to uniaxial tensile testing to high strain.
measurements: Fracture surface morphology analysis via SEM to quantify crack propagation mode (isolated vs. elongated).

Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) and Electron Backscatter Diffraction (EBSD) to map and quantify Geometrically Necessary Dislocation (GND) densities in both FCC and B2 phases at equivalent strain levels.
High-resolution TEM to assess interface coherence and topological structure.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if Set B (conventional treatment) achieves GND density convergence and elongated crack propagation comparable to Set A, or if Set A fails to show coherent interfaces and instead exhibits phase decomposition or no significant change in GND distribution compared to the untreated baseline.

Through TEM observations, we carefully characterized the evolution of the microstructure to discern the salient strengthening mechanisms generated by the SCCPs structure. Dislocation behavior at strains of 4%, 10%, and 14% in the W-based refractory HEA with the SCCPs structure are shown in Fig. 4 . Figure 4a–c, e reveal that dislocations cut through the δ-lamellae, yet are pinned by the γ ″ particles. For the coherent δ-lamellae structure, as the tensile stress increases up to the yield stress, dislocation slip occurs in the fcc matrix and involves shearing across the δ-lamellae, which indicates an early stage of the planar dislocation slip across the coherent δ/γ boundaries (Fig. 4a ). With further increase in strain to 10%, slip bands can clearly be observed across the δ-lamellae (Fig. 4b ). At a strain of 14%, shearing of the δ-lamellae by the slip bands leads to a large local shear (~40%) (Fig. 4c ), rather than the creation of a crack, which alleviates the local stress concentration. A schematic diagram of the interaction of dislocations with δ-lamellae is shown in Fig. 4d .

As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications.
